title: The LORD's Case Against His People
summary: God summons the mountains as witnesses and brings a lawsuit against Israel, recalling how he rescued them from Egypt and protected them on the way to the promised land. A worshiper asks what offering could possibly satisfy God, and the prophet answers that God has already shown what is good: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with him. The chapter ends by exposing the dishonest trade and violence of Jerusalem's wealthy and announcing the futility that will follow.
story: The book of Micah moves in three cycles, each beginning with the call to hear and each moving from judgment to hope. Chapter 6 opens the third cycle. Chapters 4 and 5 ended with the promise of a ruler from Bethlehem and a purified people; now the prophet returns to the present and asks why that purification is needed. The answer is not that God has failed Israel but that Israel has forgotten him. The chapter reaches back to the exodus and the wilderness to remind the people of their story, then comes forward to the marketplace of Micah's own day, where false weights and violence show how far they have wandered. Chapter 7 will turn this indictment into lament and then into one of the Bible's great confessions of forgiveness.
historical:
Micah worked in Judah in the late eighth century BC, under Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, while Assyria swallowed the northern kingdom and threatened the south. It was a time of real prosperity for some. Land and wealth were concentrating in the hands of the powerful, and Micah's earlier chapters accuse them of seizing fields and houses (2:1-2). Verse 16 reaches back to the ninth century, to Omri, who founded Samaria as the northern capital, and his son Ahab, whose reign with Jezebel became the Bible's byword for Baal worship and for the judicial murder of Naboth to take his vineyard (1 Kings 21). To say Jerusalem keeps the statutes of Omri is to say that the southern capital has adopted the ways of the northern one that God had just judged.

The question in verse 7 about offering a firstborn was not idle. Second Kings records that King Ahaz “sacrificed his son in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations” (2 Kings 16:3), and his grandson Manasseh did the same (2 Kings 21:6). Child sacrifice was known among Israel's neighbors, and the law had forbidden it outright (Leviticus 18:21). The worshiper's escalating offers in verses 6 and 7 mirror a religious world in which people did try to buy divine favor with ever larger gifts.
cultural:
The opening scene draws on the ancient courtroom and on treaty practice. When a king made a covenant with a vassal, the gods and the forces of nature were often called as witnesses, and Israel's covenant texts do the same with heaven and earth (Deuteronomy 32:1, Isaiah 1:2). Here the mountains and the enduring foundations of the earth are summoned to hear the LORD's case. The word for case or indictment, riv, is the ordinary word for a legal dispute, and scholars often call passages like this a covenant lawsuit.

The history in verses 4 and 5 would have been familiar. Balak king of Moab hired the seer Balaam to curse Israel, and God turned every curse into blessing (Numbers 22 to 24). Shittim was Israel's last camp east of the Jordan, and Gilgal their first camp after crossing it (Joshua 3 to 4), so the phrase from Shittim to Gilgal recalls the crossing into the land. Verses 10 and 11 move to the market. Grain was measured by the ephah, a dry measure, and silver was weighed on balance scales with stones kept in a bag. A short ephah or a light weight cheated the buyer, a sin the law named directly (Deuteronomy 25:13-16) and Amos had condemned a generation earlier (Amos 8:5). The curses of verses 14 and 15, sowing without reaping and pressing olives without using the oil, echo the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28.
literary: The chapter is built like a trial with a dialogue inside it. Verses 1 and 2 summon the witnesses; in verses 3 to 5 God speaks as the plaintiff, but instead of listing Israel's crimes he asks what he has done to weary them and recites his saving acts. Verses 6 and 7 are the defendant's reply, a series of four rising questions that move from year-old calves to thousands of rams, to rivers of oil, to a firstborn child. Verse 8 answers all four with a three-part summary that has become one of the most quoted lines in the Old Testament. The second half (verses 9 to 16) switches from dialogue to sentence: the voice of the LORD calls to the city, names its crimes, and announces a series of futility curses in which every labor fails to reach its fruit. The repeated address, My people, in verses 3 and 5 keeps the tone that of a wounded parent, not only a judge.

outline.t: God's case: remember what I have done
The worshiper's question: what offering will do
What the LORD requires: justice, mercy, humility
The city's dishonest scales and violence
The sentence: labor without fruit, the ways of Omri and Ahab

doctrines.note: The lawsuit assumes a relationship with terms: God redeemed Israel from slavery, and Israel owes him faithfulness. God's case begins with grace (verse 4) before it mentions any requirement, which is the pattern of the covenant at Sinai itself.

Verse 8 does not replace the law; it names what the law was aiming at. Justice, loyal love, and humble walking with God summarize the covenant's heart, and the dishonest scales of verses 10 and 11 show what breaking it looks like in daily trade.
Worship cannot be separated from conduct. The worshiper imagines that a large enough offering can cover anything, but the holy God asks for a life shaped by his character, not a price paid to him.

words.note: Riv, strife, dispute, or legal case. It can describe a quarrel between neighbors or a formal lawsuit, and here God himself brings a case against his people. The word frames the whole chapter as a courtroom in which God, the injured party, lays out the facts and invites a defense.

Mishpat, justice. The word covers both the act of judging and the right order that good judgment protects: fair courts, honest trade, protection for the weak. To act justly in verse 8 is to do mishpat, the very thing the rich of verse 12 have destroyed.

Chesed, kindness, mercy, loyal love. It is the steadfast, covenant-keeping love that God shows Israel, and here it is something people are to love. The BSB renders it mercy; other translations use kindness or faithfulness. It combines loyalty with generosity, doing more than the minimum a relationship requires.

Tsana, to be humble or modest, used as a verb only here in the Hebrew Bible, though a related adjective appears in Proverbs 11:2. Its exact sense is debated: many read it as humbly, others as carefully or attentively. Either way, walking with God is a way of life marked by paying attention to him rather than asserting oneself.

christ: Jesus stood in the line of prophets who refused to separate worship from justice. He twice cited Hosea's parallel saying, “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6), against critics who cared more for ritual correctness than for people (Matthew 9:13, 12:7), and he rebuked teachers who tithed their herbs but neglected “justice, mercy, and faithfulness” (Matthew 23:23), a list that closely resembles Micah 6:8. The chapter also raises a question it cannot answer on its own terms. The worshiper asks whether a firstborn could pay for sin, and Micah rightly rejects the idea; God does not want a human sacrifice from us. The New Testament's surprise is that God himself gives his own Son, not as a bribe offered by sinners but as a gift offered by God (John 3:16, Romans 8:32). The link here is thematic rather than predictive: Micah does not foresee the cross, but his question about what could cover the sin of my soul is one the gospel answers from God's side.

hard.q: Does Micah 6:8 mean God doesn't care about sacrifice and worship, only about ethics?
hard.a: Some modern readers have taken verse 8 as the prophets' rejection of ritual religion in favor of pure morality. Most interpreters think that reads too much into it. The prophets did attack worship that was cut off from justice (1 Samuel 15:22, Isaiah 1:11-17, Amos 5:21-24), but they did not abolish the temple or its offerings, and Micah elsewhere hopes for the nations streaming to the house of the LORD (4:1-2). The point of verses 6 to 8 is that no quantity of offerings can substitute for a life given to God, and that the worshiper's escalating bargaining misunderstands who God is. Walking humbly with God includes worship; it simply refuses worship as a transaction. Christians add that the sacrificial system itself pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why the church does not offer animal sacrifices, not because worship stopped mattering.

questions: God begins his case not with a list of Israel's sins but with a list of what he has done for them. Why might remembering God's past kindness be the first step in honest repentance?
The worshiper keeps raising the price of the offering. Where do you find yourself trying to make up for something with religious effort rather than a changed life?
Dishonest scales were a hidden sin, easy to justify. What are the ordinary, unnoticed ways a person or a business can act unjustly today?
